summary: Strong candidate. This is a tightly-scoped, well-tested bug fix in core cattrs disambiguation logic. The tests are layered (unit, property-based, integration) and directly validate the fix with a clear pass/fail signal. The code contains type hints, descriptive naming, and a meaningful comment—rich signals for mutation experiments. Complexity is in the sweet spot: requires library knowledge and understanding of Python idioms, but the actual change is modest. The problem description is clear enough to serve as a task prompt for an AI agent.

This is a solid PR candidate for the experiment. It touches core application code across multiple modules with real type annotations, descriptive naming, and clear tests that serve as pass/fail signals. The complexity is in the sweet spot—requires understanding the dispatch architecture but is not overwhelming. The main weakness is the extremely sparse PR description, which would make it harder to hand to an agent as a standalone task prompt without supplementing with changelog/diff context.

A well-focused bug fix with a clear test oracle, meaningful application code with type hints and docstrings, and just the right complexity level. The inheritance/singledispatch interaction is subtle enough to require genuine reasoning, but the fix is compact enough to be solvable. Strong experimental candidate.

A high-quality candidate: tightly scoped, with tests that provide clean FAIL_TO_PASS signals directly on the patched code paths, core application code with good type annotations and naming, and moderate complexity (API knowledge + multi-site fix). The main weakness is a sparse PR description that requires inferring the full task from the diff. Overall well-suited for the experiment.

This is a high-quality experimental candidate. It implements a coherent, moderately complex feature (attrib converter fallback/preference) with excellent test coverage that directly validates both behavioral modes, touches core application code dense with type hints and descriptive naming, and has a clear enough description to hand to an AI agent. The StructureHandlerNotFoundError refactor is an integral part of the feature rather than noise. All four criteria we plan to degrade (type hints, naming, comments, test surface) are richly represented, making it well-suited for measuring degradation effects.

A well-scoped, single-feature PR with excellent test coverage and clear pass/fail signals. The main weakness is a sparse PR description that would require an agent to infer the task from title and code. There is a notable parameter-name inconsistency between tests/docs (`_cattr_forbid_extra_keys`) and implementation (`_cattrs_forbid_extra_keys`) that makes this a more realistic and interesting candidate. The code touches type-annotated, well-named application logic that would expose meaningful signals under mutation. Overall a strong candidate for the experiment.

A well-focused, cleanly tested bug fix for default value handling in cattrs structuring. The test coverage is strong and the scope is tight, but the PR description is too sparse to serve as a self-contained agent prompt, and the fix is conceptually simple enough (a one-line change at its core) that it may not produce meaningful signal differences between clean and degraded codebase conditions.

This PR is unsuitable for the experiment. It is a pure import-sorting cleanup with no functional changes, no meaningful application logic touched, no test coverage of any behavior, and trivial complexity. An agent asked to re-implement this would simply run `isort` — there is no meaningful coding task here, and degrading codebase properties (type hints, naming, docstrings) would have zero impact on an agent's ability to reproduce it.
